## Pampaneira and the supramediterranean floor: snow and chestnut trees

At an altitude of 1,060 meters, Pampaneira marks the entrance to the supramediterranean floor, that ecological belt where the Mediterranean forest begins to yield ground to species that demand more moisture and cold. Centennial chestnut trees, with their twisted trunks and broad canopies, dominate the slopes surrounding the village, accompanied by Pyrenean oaks that cling to the deepest shaded areas. The automatic station of the SAIH Network (Automatic Hydrological Information System) installed in the municipality records an average annual precipitation of 700 millimeters, a figure that far exceeds the records of Órgiva, just fifteen kilometers down the valley. This moisture, combined with the altitude, completely transforms the landscape and the daily life of its inhabitants.

Winter in Pampaneira has a harshness that surprises those who only know the Alpujarra from summer photographs. Snowfalls occur between three and five days a year, enough to cover the slate roofs and conical chimneys with a white layer that transforms the image of the village. The same SAIH Network station has recorded lows of five degrees below zero in January, temperatures that turn public fountains into ice sculptures and force neighbors to protect outdoor pipes. The chestnut trees, however, are perfectly adapted to this regime: they need the winter cold to complete their reproductive cycle and produce the chestnuts that for centuries were a staple food in the region.

Transhumance remains alive in the Valle del Poqueira, although with fewer flocks than in past decades. The livestock farmers who each spring ascend with their sheep and goats from the lower areas to the high-altitude pastures have noticed changes they attribute to global warming. According to testimonies collected by the Asociación de Ganaderos de la Alpujarra, spring grass now appears ten days earlier than in the year 2000, an advance that alters the traditional calendar for moving up to the mountain passes. That decade of difference may seem minor in absolute terms, but for a shepherd planning transhumance weeks in advance, it represents a significant adjustment in flock management and the availability of fresh pasture.

The supramediterranean floor represented by Pampaneira functions as a natural laboratory where the effects of climate change on mountain ecosystems can be clearly observed. The chestnut trees, which require constant moisture and summers that are not excessively hot, show signs of water stress in the driest years, when their leaves yellow prematurely and chestnut production declines. The Pyrenean oaks, for their part, better withstand climatic variability thanks to their deep root system, but they also suffer from the lack of spring rainfall. The automatic station in Pampaneira provides fundamental data for understanding these dynamics, with time series that allow the evolution of temperatures and precipitation to be compared over recent decades.

The traditional economy of Pampaneira has historically revolved around these forest and livestock resources. The chestnut, harvested in autumn, was consumed fresh, dried to preserve it through the winter, or ground to obtain flour used to make porridges and subsistence breads. The oaks supplied excellent quality firewood for homes and timber for the construction of beams and farming tools. This intimate relationship between the village and its forest environment explains the current physiognomy of the landscape: a mosaic of cultivated chestnut groves, patches of oak in the wildest areas, and irrigated terraces in the vicinity of the urban core, where the water from the irrigation ditches allows the cultivation of vegetables and fruit trees despite the altitude.

The data from the Pampaneira meteorological station are especially valuable for understanding the climatic transition that occurs over just forty kilometers of road. While Motril records around three hundred clear days a year and an average annual temperature close to eighteen degrees, Pampaneira endures winters with frequent frosts and mild summers that rarely exceed thirty degrees. This thermal difference of more than ten degrees in the annual average translates into a succession of bioclimatic floors that turns the A-4130 into a first-order ecological transect. The traveler ascending from the coast can observe in a single day how the plant species, vernacular architecture, and even the crops change, each adapted to the specific conditions of its altitude.

The Asociación de Ganaderos de la Alpujarra insists that the advance of spring grass is not a mere meteorological curiosity, but an early indicator of deeper transformations. Transhumant shepherds depend on a natural calendar that has remained stable for generations, and any alteration in this rhythm forces a rethinking of routes, shearing dates, and breeding periods. Some livestock farmers have begun moving up to the mountain passes of Sierra Nevada a week earlier than was customary, while others maintain the traditional dates and accept that their flocks will find pastures that are already overgrown and less nutritious. The accumulated experience of these professionals of the land constitutes a source of information that complements the instrumental records of the SAIH Network.

Pampaneira summarizes in its municipal territory the essence of the Alpujarra supramediterranean floor: a transition territory where the deciduous forest replaces the Mediterranean scrubland, where snow becomes a recurrent phenomenon, and where extensive livestock farming keeps alive land uses that have their roots in the Andalusian era. The chestnut trees surrounding the village are not just a landscape element; they represent a cultural and economic heritage that has shaped the identity of this part of the Alpujarra. The January snowfalls, the frosts recorded by the automatic station, and the spring advance documented by the livestock farmers draw a complex scenario, where tradition and climate change coexist in an increasingly delicate balance.
